<meta>This is the opening page of the preface to the 1881 reproduction of the Lapidary of King Alfonso X. The tone is formal and celebratory, typical of 19th-century Spanish scholarship.</meta>

# PROLOGUE.

## DON JOSÉ FERNANDEZ MONTAÑA, PRIEST, TO THOSE WHO SHALL READ.

### I.

We must call one of the most celebrated and precious manuscripts kept in the famous Library of San Lorenzo del Escorial (1) an inexhaustible mine of light and wealth for the sciences and the arts. Our historians hardly mention it, because they had no news of it other than the title with which antiquity baptized it, namely: *The Lapidary <note>A "Lapidary" is a book about the properties, virtues, and medicinal or magical uses of gemstones and minerals.</note> of King Alfonso the Wise of Castile*. And in past centuries there was no lack of those who named it, sometimes the "Lapidary of the Library of San Lorenzo," and other times the "Lapidary of Don Diego de Mendoza." Consequently, the well-known artist Don Antonio Selfa deserves the gratitude of the scientific world, having just reproduced the excellent *Book of Stones* with great fidelity and photo-lithographic mastery; and above all, Mr. Don Hipólito Rodrigáñez, the diligent and learned director of periodical publications, whose love and protection for the publishing enterprise was constant and resolute from the first thought of delivering the codex <note>A "codex" is an ancient manuscript in book form rather than a scroll.</note> to the public domain.

---

(1) Let the impartial and judicious reader remember here that the most celebrated and truly royal Library of the Escorial owes its birth and scientific and literary riches to the great Monarch Don Philip II, and how each of those codices and those incunabula <note>original: "incunables" — books printed before the year 1501, during the infancy of the printing press.</note> editions is crying out with a loud voice that the son of Charles V was a king who was a protector of letters, a friend of sciences, and a lover of all wisdom.

<summary>In this prologue, the priest José Fernandez Montaña introduces the first photographic reproduction of the "Lapidary of Alfonso the Wise," praising the scholars and artists who made the manuscript accessible to the public.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the preface to the study of the Escorial Lapidary, establishing the historical context and royal patronage of the manuscript.</meta>

# PROLOGUE

The purpose of these pages is to briefly determine the origin of the Escorial Lapidary <note>A "Lapidary" is a treatise on the magical and medicinal properties of gemstones and minerals</note>; its history; its value and incalculable literary, artistic, and scientific merit; concluding with the proper historical and laudatory remembrance of the wise Prince who ordered its translation into the Castilian language and made it a precious heritage for the Spanish people.

The *Book of Stones* was born into the Castilian language in the second half of the 13th century. This is evidenced by the first page of the Index of the Lapidary itself, which features a most curious portrait of the Wise King and the following words, printed here with complete fidelity. They read as follows:

> "Here begins the book of the forms and images that are in the heavens, and of the virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the inherent powers or properties of the stones</note>, and of the works that proceed from them in the bodies that are below the heaven of the moon, which the very high and honored Don Alfonso, lover of sciences and knowledge, by the grace of God King of Castile, Toledo, Leon, Galicia, Seville, Cordoba, Murcia, Jaen, and the Algarve, ordered to be composed from the books of the ancient philosophers. And son of the very honored King Don Ferdinand and Queen Lady Beatrice. *And this book was begun in the 25th year of his reign. And in the Era of Caesar, in one thousand three hundred and fourteen years. And that of our Lord Jesus Christ, in one thousand two hundred and seventy-six years. And it was finished in the 27th year of his reign. And the Era of Caesar, in one thousand three hundred and 17 years. And that of our Lord Jesus Christ, in one thousand two hundred and seventy-nine years.*" <note>The "Era of Caesar" or Spanish Era was a dating system used in the Iberian Peninsula that begins in 38 BC; hence the discrepancy between the dates.</note>

The Index from which we have copied this paragraph—which establishes the date of our Lapidary—forms a separate codex, occupies a place immediately alongside the *Book of Stones* in the Escorial Library, and teaches us the parts of which it consisted, which were undoubtedly no fewer than eleven; today all, except one, are unknown or lost.

This very obscure manuscript gives a detailed account of the eleven parts, declaring the subjects contained in each and the names of the sages who composed them. The first "speaks of the images and of their works that are made in the stones." Its author was *Abolays* <note>Abolays is the Spanish transliteration of an Arabic name, likely a scholar of Chaldean or Arabic sources</note>, of whom we shall speak later. "And the second is by *Timtim*, who speaks of another manner of images." The third is attributed to *Pythagoras*, and likewise treats other classes of figures in stones. From *Iluz* comes the fourth part of the Lapidary, or Lapidaries of the Wise King, explaining the same subject matter through various paths. At the head of the fifth

# PROLOGUE

two authors appear, namely: *Belyenus* <note>Often identified as Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed magician</note> and the aforementioned *Iluz*. The points declared therein are also another type of images "which are made in the stones by the planets when they are in their dignities <term>dignities: the positions in the zodiac where a planet's influence is considered strongest</term> and hours." The sixth part belongs to *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the Roman 'Natural History'</note>, *Belyenus*, and other ancient sages. In it are described the images "that are made in stones by making rings from them." *Utatit* <note>Likely the mathematician and astronomer Thabit ibn Qurra</note> is the author of the seventh part, in which we are given an account and reason for seven images "that are made by the seven planets in seven specific stones." Our codex calls the author of the eighth part *Ragiel* <note>Likely the archangel or sage Raziel, associated with mystical secrets</note>. "It speaks of 22 images that must be made on specific stones." The ninth part is by *Jacoth*, and its subject matter was the waters and muds that are necessary in this work of the stones. The author of the tenth of those parts was named *Aly*, and in it "he speaks of how stones must be engraved and of other rules that are necessary in this science." The eleventh and final part of the famous Lapidaries <note>Treatises on the properties and powers of gemstones</note> that were the object of study and attention for the Wise Castilian King <note>Alfonso X of Castile, 1221–1284</note>, is presented without an author's name. It deals with the images "that are found already formed in the stones."

The celebrated Escorial codex, which today comes to light for the greater joy and increase of knowledge, contains only the first of all the aforementioned parts or lapidaries. In its entirety, it forms the treatise called that of *Abolays* <note>A legendary figure often cited in medieval Spanish texts as a source of Babylonian stone-lore</note>, and is divided in turn into three different parts. The first includes the detailed description of three hundred and sixty stones that constitute a rich catalog of scientific ideas and general knowledge. It is subdivided into twelve minor parts that are in perfect harmony with the signs of the Zodiac. The purpose of the second part is to point out the singular virtues <note>In this context, 'virtues' refers to the inherent medicinal or magical powers of the minerals</note> of each stone, thanks to solar influence, explaining in passing the figures of the stars and their power over minerals. Finally, the third part offers the primary causes of the rare phenomena produced in the stones by the planets of the firmament, referred to there by the name of the *eighth heaven* <note>In medieval cosmology, the eighth heaven (or sphere) was the realm of the fixed stars, situated beyond the spheres of the seven planets</note>. Following the lapidary codex of the famous *Abolays*, the manuscript continues with the *Treatise on the stones or Lapidary of Mahomad-Aben-Quich*, a book held in high esteem among the scholars of the Arabic and Jewish people throughout the Middle Ages. The scientific work of *Quich*, as the Prologue beginning it notes, was written "according to the knowledge in the books of the wise" and as a result of experience. It is organized in its entirety in alphabetical order, following the requirement and custom of Mahometan <note>An archaic term for Islamic</note> science of those centuries. The description of the

# PROLOGUE

stones, their natural color, virtue <note>original: "virtud"; refers to the inherent medicinal or magical power believed to reside within the stone</note>, properties, nature, and their relationships with stars and planets, constitute the essential matter placed before our eyes by the unknown book of *Mahomad-Aben-Quich* <note>Likely a reference to Muhammad ibn Qais</note>.

No writer of weight in these disciplines, nor true friend of wisdom, when reaching this descriptive part of the famous *Lapidary books of King Alfonso X* <note>Alfonso X "The Wise" of Castile (reigned 1252–1284), who oversaw a massive project of translating scientific and legal texts</note>, fails to call the attention of naturalists and mineralogists to the astrological influence that the ancients imagined over terrestrial things. For nothing is indifferent in the history of the sciences (1).

The graceful and elegant Prologue of the *Lapidary* teaches us how, in past and rather remote times, the sages of the Eastern regions wrote books in which they treat and speak much of all natural things, particularly of noble and base stones, both precious and of little value; declaring their virtues and properties alongside the physical and chemical characteristics of each and every one of them. It is added in that same place that among the men of knowledge who worked most on this matter, one deserves very singular remembrance: he who went by the name Abolays <note>A scholar often cited as the primary source or translator for the first part of the Lapidary, credited with finding the original "Chaldean" manuscript</note>, a learned professor and teacher in the law of the Moors and a great lover of the country and sciences of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, traditionally associated by medieval writers with the origins of astronomy and magic</note>, being himself of the lineage and blood of those natives. Jewish and Arabic libraries offer none too abundant accounts of the life of this celebrated naturalist; we will note here in passing that from an early age he found himself drawn by a marked affection to scrutinize the books and natural sciences of the Chaldean sages; for in that land, according to Saracens <note>A medieval term for Arabs or Muslims</note> and Jews, the best and most celebrated scholars in the world were born and studied.

Now then; the renowned Abolays had a friend whom he loved with singular affection and care. Almost ignored by history, it is related that this friend demonstrated his gratitude and responded to the esteem of the Chaldean sage by gifting him books on Mineralogy and other natural sciences; and among them, there came into his power the excellent *Lapidary* "which speaks of three hundred and sixty stones" <note>original: "que fabla de trezientas sesaenta piedras"</note>. Abolays rejoiced exceedingly at such good fortune and precious find, and seeing the *Book of the Stones* in his hands, he read it and read it again,

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the provenance of the manuscript, explaining how the scholar Abolays translated the text from "Chaldean" into Arabic and how, after a period of being lost following his death, the book eventually found its way to the court of King Alfonso X.</meta>

...studying it with such attention and diligence that he finished by translating it from the Chaldean language <note>original: "caldeo"; in this period, the term often referred to Syriac or Aramaic, languages of ancient scholarship</note> into the tongue of Arabia <note>Arabic</note>; proving, through personal experience, the truth and accuracy of the things and teachings written there. The death of this Moorish naturalist <note>Refers to Abolays, the scholar mentioned on the previous page</note> was the death—at least temporarily—of our *Lapidary*, for from then on it fell into such neglect that it was as if lost for a time, "until God willed that it should come into the hands of the noble King Don Alfonso, son of the very noble King Don Fernando and Queen Doña Beatriz" <note>Alfonso X was the son of Ferdinand III of Castile and Elizabeth (Beatriz) of Swabia</note>.

## II.

Now let the diligent reader recall that surprising scientific and literary movement, and the most laudable eagerness to give protection and life to letters and arts in the court of the Wise King, which had already begun, and had even gained no small momentum, in the palaces of Saint Ferdinand and Doña Berenguela <note>Ferdinand III and his mother, Berengaria of Castile, who laid the groundwork for the cultural flourishing of the 13th century</note>. Bring to mind the names of so many workers celebrated then in the field of knowledge: some Christians; others Jews and Muslims. The latter came from Eastern regions, filled with a rationalistic spirit of antiquity; the former were born and held in higher esteem under the warmth of the Christian faith in Western lands. Place before your eyes Master Guillen, Master Johan d’Aspa, Master Fernando of Toledo, Master Bernardo the Arab, the cleric Garci-Perez, Rabbi Judah Mosca, Iacub Hatolaitolah, Rabbi Dor Abrahem, and so many other tireless searchers and composers of books, systems, and natural disciplines in the royal palaces <term>alcázares</term> <note>From the Spanish "alcázar," a type of Moorish castle or palace</note> of Alfonso the Wise. You should know then that from one of them—a citizen of Toledo, to be more precise—our Prince obtained the admirable *Book of Stones*. Once the *Lapidary* was in the royal hands of the Wise Alfonso, it passed immediately into those of Judah Mosca the Younger, a Jewish physician, and to those of Garci-Perez...

<meta>This page continues the history of the manuscript's translation from Arabic into the Spanish vernacular under the patronage of Alfonso X, and traces its physical journey through historical libraries to its current home in El Escorial.</meta>

# PROLOGUE

...priest, both being very knowledgeable in the nature and movement of the stars and the Arabic and Latin languages. And having heard the Wise Prince of the great scientific wonders that the *Lapidary* <note>A "Lapidary" is a treatise on the properties and virtues of precious stones</note> contained, "he ordered it translated from Arabic into the Castilian tongue so that men might understand it better and know how to profit more from it" <note>original: "mandólo trasladar del arábigo en lengua castellana porque los homes lo entendiesen meyor et se sopiesen dél mas aprovechar"</note>. This version was completed in the year 1250; that is, in the "second year after the noble King Don Ferdinand, his father, won the city of Seville" <note>Ferdinand III captured Seville from the Almohad Caliphate in 1248</note>.

In the palaces of kings and magnates, cherished by all and held in great price and esteem, the *Book of Stones* passed through the 14th and 15th centuries until the 16th, during which it appeared in the excellent and rich library of Don Diego de Mendoza <note>A renowned Spanish diplomat, historian, and book collector</note>. Upon the death of such an illustrious man, all his books—not seized, but by a most just contract—passed into the power of King Philip II, who succeeded in greatly increasing the never-sufficiently praised Library of El Escorial, thanks to so many magnificent volumes on varied subjects and written in all languages. Among them, and by this route, the *Lapidary of Don Alfonso the Wise of Castile* came to take a place of honor on the Escorial shelves of Juan de Herrera <note>The architect of El Escorial who also organized its library</note>, never to leave there again.

And could such a valued manuscript, by chance, be the very one in which the son of Saint Ferdinand read and studied? All the critics and scholars who have handled it do not doubt it. For the character of the handwriting, the form and face of the language, the mastery with which the capital letters are drawn, the <term>indumentaria: the styles of dress and costume depicted in the manuscript's illustrations</term>, the variety of instruments displayed there, and finally all the intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics of such a famous manuscript, prove it to be a work of the 13th century. Add to all this the great care with which it is crafted, the elegance of its initials, the industry of the drawings, and the brilliance of the coloring, and we shall remain within the truth by asserting that this, and no other, must have been the original *Lapidary* prepared for the use and recreation of the Monarch, surnamed The Wise.

It is a difficult business now to briefly declare the subjects and disciplines contained in the *Lapidary*. For such a famous book becomes like a true encyclopedia in which all knowledge is found; a very full and well-tended artistic-scientific seedbed; a focus of clearest light; a projector of many splendors upon all the branches of the tree of science. And indeed, in the *Book of Stones*, the properties, virtues, and colors of infinite minerals appear explained; their marvelous effects, simple—

Experts confirm it is the original 13th-century codex based on its linguistic style and artistic illuminations.</summary>

IX
-># PROLOGUE<-

...[valu]ably used, or in combination; utilized in their natural state, or dissolved and reduced to powder; all of which is of great interest to the physical, chemical, mineralogical, and medicinal sciences. Within its pages, the stones and minerals—studied with scrupulous analysis and a natural inclination—are called and cited by their proper Arabic, Chaldean <note>referring to Aramaic or Neo-Babylonian sources</note>, Greek, Latin, and Castilian names; a feature that lovers of Philology <note>the study of language in historical sources</note> will surely look upon with favor. The *Lapidary* <note>a treatise on the properties of stones</note> also provides an account of the kingdoms, peoples, mountains, rivers, and seas where the stones it explains are found; a subject of particular interest to the diligent historian and geographer.

Nor is there a lack of an astonishing multitude of varied figures: costumes of most brilliant colors; countless drawings of religious and secular figures, birds and diverse creatures of sea and land; furniture, instruments, vessels, and numerous other objects. All of this serves as a spur and incentive to the laudable curiosity of those who devote themselves to the study of art, industry, navigation, and universal history, both ecclesiastical and secular. The peculiar character of the manuscript has already been noted above, particularly its capital letters, the unusual paths of its spelling, and finally, the overall appearance of the script, the forms of which paleographers <note>scholars who study ancient and historical handwriting</note> will find of great use. Above all, the stability, fixity, and ease that our Castilian language already displayed at that time deserves great attention and close examination—not forgetting the particular syllabic separation of adverbs, nor the straight and well-defined paths of the other parts of speech. All these things, when well observed and considered, will redound to the benefit and grace of the national language. Nor do the phenomena of minerals, as the *Lapidary* itself notes and commands us to observe, fail to demand due contemplation; for from this might well arise a greater light upon the relationships between organic and inorganic Chemistry, thereby expanding and strengthening the foundations of Medicine. There, in short, to conclude once and for all, all sciences, arts, letters, and paths of human wisdom can find most savory and profitable nourishment.

-># PROLOGUE<-

## III.

Such is the value and worth of the ancient and monumental work that the tenth of the Alfonsos, surnamed "the Wise," left to us translated into the Spanish language. Such a gift, of such high esteem and literary richness, most justly demands special remembrance and praise for the august Prince who bequeathed such valuable jewels to men of the future. On November 23rd of the year 1223 <note>Historical records typically place Alfonso’s birth in 1221; the author here follows a specific manuscript tradition</note>, the imperial city of Toledo saw him born—the cradle of so many and such illustrious men, and of so many and most pleasing memories (1). In the very ancient and most noble <term>Seville</term> <note>a major city in southern Spain, recently reconquered from the Moors at the time</note>, a city without rival in beauty and poetry, they swore him in as King of <term>Castile and León</term> <note>the two primary Christian kingdoms united under his father</note> on June 2, 1252, at twenty-three years of age; and there he also breathed his last breath of life on April 4, 1284. The heroic virtues of <term>Saint Ferdinand</term> <note>Ferdinand III, Alfonso's father, who united the kingdoms and was later canonized</note> demanded and deserved such a successor to the Spanish throne; nor could any other but Don Alfonso the Wise dry the tears that the kingdom then shed, mourning the death of the great conqueror, warrior, and saint.

The wisdom, judgment, power, and tact of the Crown Prince immediately sowed hope and consolation in all the provinces of the Peninsula. And seeing in the Wise King courage, genius, industry, and experience, the people considered themselves most fortunate. Our Iberian nation has always understood too well how a King of such gifts and qualities—who knows how to uphold the laws of God in one hand and those of the fatherland in the other—is like an omnipotent being, capable of the most heroic deeds. And if the history of the reign of Alfonso the Wise offers, like all human things, scenes full of darkness ...

(Don Alfonso.)

-># PROLOGUE<-

and gloom, let them be held not as political ignorance or the King’s errors, but as the lashes of <term>Divine Providence</term> <note>a theological concept suggesting that God intervenes in human history</note> upon the guilt of the people. For Kings also have a King, and nations have their Purgatory or their Paradise.

The history of the Castilian Wise King is a most eloquent lesson for princes and the powerful. As the heir and lord of a grand, vast, and opulent kingdom, his counsel and friendship were sought by kin and strangers alike; friends paid him esteem and homage, while his rivals offered him fear and respect. Upon such high peaks of wealth and power had a <term>holy King</term> <note>referring to his father, Saint Ferdinand III</note> seated Spain! But oh, the littleness and wretchedness of all things human! Alfonso X, despite all his opulence, genius, and wisdom, was destined to lose friends and gain fierce and resentful enemies. He saw faith broken and national agreements torn down; tributary Princes took up arms against his crown; his most beloved vassals incited towns and raised armies against his royal scepter; and to crown these calamities, he saw his own brothers, and even Prince Don Sancho—surnamed "the Brave"—turn away and turn their backs on him <note>Prince Sancho led a rebellion against his father in 1282 over succession rights</note>. The verdict of history, however, has not yet decided what the Wise King’s place should be in the theater of human greatness: let no one wonder, then, that we, along with solemn authors, continue to call him magnanimous, brave, majestic, and by excellence, <term>the Wise</term>.

Indeed, the liberality and nobility of the Castilian Wise King were shown marvelously during the thirty-two stormy years of his reign. Whether the winds were fair or foul, with kin or foreigners, with children and brothers, with friends and enemies, his magnanimity and generous heart remained the same and without limits for all. Look to the specific history of Spain, which offers us the son of Saint Ferdinand as great in every one of his public deeds, and most worthy toward all men, both powerful and lowly.

His magnificence was fully realized, and in such a way that he knew how to despise the material treasures of gold and silver to eagerly acquire the glory of fame. And he did not repent; for at the sound and shadow of that fame, nothing less than the <term>Empire of Germany</term> <note>the Holy Roman Empire; Alfonso spent much of his reign and wealth pursuing the title of Holy Roman Emperor</note> came knocking at the gates of his <term>fortresses</term> <note>original: "alcázares," a term for Moorish-style fortified palaces</note>. In this way, the glory and power of the imperial and very noble <term>House of Austria</term> <note>the Habsburg dynasty, which would later rule Spain</note> was born from the Castilian Wise King. Nor was courage or bravery lacking in the tenth King among the Alfonsos, who so skillfully directed in person many bloody struggles and combats, achieving, sword in hand, most glorious victories. Throughout all the stages of his mortal life, not even excepting the years of old age, he flew with great courage and heroism to the battlefields. Solid devotion and erudition of great height and variety: these were the two poles upon which the thoughts of the son of <term>Saint Ferdinand</term> <note>King Ferdinand III of Castile, Alfonso's father, known for his massive territorial gains against the Moors</note> turned. ## IV.

Having found qualities of such high esteem in the son of Saint Ferdinand, it should now be an easy task to briefly demonstrate his great wisdom. That well-known saying among Spaniards, so often repeated by serious writers, does not belong to Alfonso X of Castile—namely: "If God had asked my advice when He created the universe, I would have made it differently." This was a crude and tedious joke by <term>Pedro IV the Ceremonious</term> <note>King of Aragon (1336–1387), known for his complex court etiquette</note>; it was unjustly attached to the pen of <term>Zurita</term> <note>Jerónimo Zurita, a major 16th-century Spanish historian</note>, passing from his work into the public consciousness. Both were corrected with boldness and courage by the <term>Marquis of Mondejar</term> in his *Historical Memoirs*. Nor were <term>Mariana, Feijóo, and Father Florez</term> <note>influential Spanish historians and thinkers from the 16th to 18th centuries</note> correct in saying of the Wise King: "While he contemplates the heavens, he lost the earth" <note>original Latin: *Dum cœlum considerat, terram amissit*</note>. This is equivalent to believing that the thorny art of governing was unknown to our King. For, in truth, he who knew how to compose nothing less than the immortal works of the *Royal Charter* <note>original: *Fuero Real*</note>, the *Mirror* <note>original: *Especulo*</note>, and the *Seven Parts* <note>original: *Las Partidas*; one of the most important legal codes in Western history</note> must have fully understood political matters and the paths for directing nations. And as for diminishing, even by a single point, the supreme wisdom of King Alfonso X, such a thing is not permitted for obvious reasons by <term>Nicolás Antonio</term>, <term>Velázquez</term>, <term>Mondejar</term>, or <term>Sarmiento</term> <note>a list of prominent Spanish scholars and bibliographers</note>,

More distorted and less Spanish is the opinion of those who call King Alfonso X "the Wise," but only through the grace and work of <term>Muslim</term> <note>original: *muslimicos*</note> and Jewish learning and teachers. This is an unfounded opinion, typical of people whose understanding tends to sail by every course and at the whim of every wind. It is a foolish and foreign way of thinking, which finds no difference between the Bible and the Talmud, between the <term>tiara</term> <note>the Pope's crown, representing the Catholic Church</note> and the turban, between Jesus Christ and Muhammad. To argue in our time that only Moors and Jews transformed the tenth of the Alfonsos into a scholar requires a total ignorance of the nature and life of the Spanish people under the yoke of the <term>Saracens</term> <note>a medieval term for Arabs or Muslims</note>. Note first and with great emphasis—to settle this question—that Alfonso the Wise undoubtedly received his early religious and literary education not in the lands or schools of Moors and rabbis, but in **Galicia**. At that time, Galicia was a region entirely nourished and sustained by the Catholic Church and Christian science (1). Let the impartial critic also remember here that Alfonso the Wise was the son of a saint <note>referring to King Ferdinand III, "the Saint"</note> and that he learned the worship of the one God and a love for science in the home of his grandmother, **Lady Berenguela**. She was a most devout and highly educated woman, a friend of piety and letters, of whom we know that "she took pleasure in men of the court who knew well how to compose poetry <note>original: *trovar*</note> and in <term>minstrels</term> <note>original: *ioglares*</note> who knew well how to play instruments." Let us also keep fixed in our memory the immense influence of lyric-poetic compositions, saturated with patriotic love and Catholic civilization. These were owed not to the Rabbinic Kabbalah, nor to the Quran, but to the Christian <term>troubadours</term>, both Provençal and Catalan, whom the royal author of the *Praises to Holy Mary* <note>original: *Loores á Santa Maria*</note> neither ignored nor overlooked.

Villanueva in his *Literary Journey*, Milá in his *Precious Observations on Popular Poetry*, and Millot in the *Literary History of the Troubadours*, along with various other ancient and modern critics, have demonstrated with total clarity and force how in Catalonia, Asturias, Galicia, Portugal, and many regions of our Spain in the 12th and 13th centuries, there existed a perennial study and development of popular and religious poetry and songs.

We cannot, nor do we wish to, leave this subject without calling the attention of our critics and those who love our national glory to the wealthy and hidden monuments found within the ancient altarpieces of our Gothic cathedrals—raised by Christian artists and masters—and within our archives and libraries. For the state of the divine art of painting in our Spain during the latter half of the century of **Saint Ferdinand** and **Don Alfonso the Wise** is much to be admired. In our view, the lovers of national arts have not focused intently enough on this point, and we believe that all the attention of current and future critics and artists should be directed there. For it is necessary to understand that such artistic beauties did not create themselves; they have authors, and these must have been Spaniards. It is probable that by beginning to trace the path of the general history of the Peninsula and the particular chronicles of religious houses, following the modest <term>illuminators</term> <note>artists who decorated manuscripts</note>, painters, and draftsmen of the 13th and 14th centuries, we may find new *Cimabues*, *Giottos*, *Taddeo Gaddis*, and *Angelicos* <note>The author compares Spanish artists to these famous masters of the Italian Renaissance to emphasize their quality</note> for the history of the arts in Spain.

This reflects a medieval theological sentiment regarding the Virgin Mary’s power of intercession with her Son</note> These books are all of great value, and so numerous that the authors have had to classify them into groups to provide some account of them. It would be a never-ending tale to attempt the analysis and description of all the books of **Alfonso the Wise** here. There are mineralogical, astronomical, legal, historical, poetic, and philosophical works. Not all of these can find a place here; only those that deal purely with the natural sciences; and without making a detailed study of each, which would be a task of many volumes, but rather citing them almost simply by their names.

There are at least 21 natural-scientific treatises by Don Alfonso X that modern critics have identified. Any one of these works would be enough to place the title of **The Wise** upon the crown of such an admirable Sovereign. At the head of so many such treatises, we shall place the *Lapidary of Abolays* <note>A treatise on the properties of stones and their relationship to the stars</note> with the other work by *Aben-Quich* added by the translators, as we mentioned previously.

After the *Lapidary* come the *Astronomical Tables*, arranged according to the meridian of Toledo and the date of the royal author's accession to the Castilian throne.

Next follows the *Book of the Eighth Sphere and its 47 Figures*. It is a translation from Arabic and Chaldean, attributed to Yehuda ben Moses <note>referred to in the text as Iehudah-ha-Cohen</note>, a legal scholar or judge of the <term>aljamas</term> <note>Aljama: an autonomous community of Jews or Muslims living under Christian rule in medieval Spain</note> of the Wise King. A principal role in this work was taken by Guillen-fi de Remon d'Aspa, who was a clergyman to our King.

Then appears the *Book of the Alcora* or the *Book of the Sphere*. "King Don Alfonso, son of the very noble King Don Fernando and Queen Doña Beatrice, ordered it translated from Arabic into the Castilian language by Master Johan Daspa, his clergyman, and Yehuda ben Moses, his physician, in the era of one thousand two hundred and ninety-seven years." <note>The "Spanish Era" calendar differs from the Gregorian; the year 1297 mentioned here corresponds to 1259 AD</note>

The *Round Astrolabe* and the *Flat Astrolabe* follow next, both composed by Rabbi Zag of Toledo <note>Isaac ibn Sid, a famous Jewish astronomer and a primary collaborator in Alfonso's scientific circle</note>, a famous astronomer of those times.

Master Fernando of Toledo and Abu-Isahak-Ben-Yahia Azarcall <note>Arzachel (c. 1029–1087), a preeminent Arab astronomer from Toledo whose work influenced later European science</note> fulfilled this honorable commission. To make it complete, the same Rabbi Zag of Toledo received the royal command.

The codices of the National Library subsequently offer another book also brought into our beautiful Castilian language by the will of the Wise King. It is titled the *Book of the Plates*, and it «speaks of how a man can make a plate for each planet; and how a man can make one plate for all the planets.»

After this last treatise come six more, nearly all of them composed by the aforementioned Zag of Toledo, thanks to the direction and protection of Don Alfonso. They are christened with these names: *The Quadrant*, made «when the era of our Lord Jesus Christ stood at the year 1277.» *Stone of the Shadow* <note>A treatise on sundials</note>, composed, as the Wise King notes, «because we did not find a book on the matter of the stone of the shadow that was complete.» *The Water Clock*, also newly worked upon by our King, «because what we found written in the books made by the ancient sages was lacking,» he says. The treatise *Of the Mercury Clock* <note>original: "argent vivo," literally "living silver" or quicksilver</note> was arranged «by the art of the book made by Iran the philosopher, in which he speaks of how heavy things can be lifted.» In the *Prologue of the Palace of the Hours*, the Wise Don Alfonso says: «we commanded the aforementioned Rabbi Zag to make this book in which he shows how this Palace should be made.» With the *Atazir* <note>A method for calculating astrological planetary houses and directions</note> and the *Candle Clock*, the mentioned codex in which the aforementioned treatises are recorded concludes.

Modern scholars also cite, as oriental books of natural science—

***

(1) The curious reader knows better than we do that whoever wishes for detailed descriptions of the contents of each of these scientific treatises by the Wise King should know and consult the Arabic Libraries, especially that of Casiri; as well as Nicolás Antonio, Bayer, and the originals held in the Libraries of Madrid, Toledo, and the Escorial. See primarily in the National Library the codices marked L. 97 and 184: T. 273 and K. 196: and in the Escorial, that of Q. III-26.

-># PROLOGUE<-

...[gene]ral, translated into Spanish by royal decree of Don Alfonso: the *Canons of Al-Battani* <note>original: "Cánones de Albatem," the astronomical tables of the 9th-century Arab scientist Al-Battani</note>, the *Complete Book on the Judgment of the Stars*, and the *Book of the Three Crosses*. Almost all of these deal with judicial astrology <term>Judicial Astrology: The practice of predicting the fate of individuals or nations based on the positions of celestial bodies</term>, along with other matters of nature. The first is originally attributed to Muhammad ibn Jābir <note>original: "Mahomad-ben-Giaber," referring again to Al-Battani</note>. Master Gil de Tebaldos and Pedro del Real translated the second into Latin, not counting the translation by Alvaro Hispano, a servant of Don Alfonso. The third appears to be the work of Ubayd Allah <note>original: "Obéid-Allah," likely referring to the 10th-century scholar Ubayd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn al-Sari</note>; it treats the four superior planets and the influences of the stars on subjects, kings, and kingdoms. The translation was performed by Juan d’Aspa and Moses ha-Kohen <note>original: "Mosseh-ha-Cohen," a prominent Jewish physician and translator at the Alfonsine court</note>.

We have reached the end of our journey, and along the way we have been able to contemplate the son of Saint Ferdinand <note>King Ferdinand III of Castile, Alfonso's father</note> as the head and living image of the Spanish people. He marches with a firm step along the paths of Christian wisdom—gathering, it is true, from the fields of the incomplete Arabic and Jewish civilizations whatever fruits and flowers might embellish and serve as adornment for Castilian letters. Yet he did so without ever placing, even for a moment, the knowledge of the Cross behind the cabalistic <term>Cabalistic: Here referring to esoteric or mystical Jewish thought</term> and heretical reasoning of the Saracens <term>Saracens: A medieval term for Muslims</term>. He purged and cleansed Hebrew-Arabic science with great discernment in the divine crucible of the Catholic faith. In every way, he increased and strengthened that majestic artistic, scientific, and literary tradition which, in those times, boasted the giant cathedrals of Burgos and Toledo as its foundations, and two centuries later, the incomparable temple of Seville as its crown. Finally, we consider the Castilian Prince to be showing, with full right and imprinted upon his noble soul, those royal attributes of *magnificent, majestic, brave, magnanimous, and wise*.

# REPORT

### OF THE

# ROYAL ACADEMY OF HISTORY

->Most Excellent Sir:<-

In order for the Academy to properly fulfill the report requested by the General Directorate of Public Instruction, Agriculture, and Commerce regarding the photochromolithographic <term>Photochromolithography: A 19th-century color printing process that combined photography with lithography to create highly accurate reproductions of artworks and manuscripts</term> edition of the famous codex of the *Lapidary* <note>original: "Lapidario," a treatise describing the medical and astrological properties of stones and gems</note>, which belonged to King Alfonso X and currently resides in the Library of the Escorial, the undersigned members have taken the opportunity to examine the original manuscript there and compare it minutely with the printed version. The idea of this publication recommends itself.

The priest Don José Fernandez Montaña, our Correspondent, the well-reputed artist Don Antonio Selfa, and Don Hipólito Rodrigáñez y Sagasta have conceived the laudable and fruitful project of publishing—by the prodigious means of photography and chromolithography—the most celebrated and precious codices of the Escorial, providing a service of utmost importance and significance to letters and the arts. They have begun, with a most fortunate choice, with a unique and singular codex commissioned by the wise King Alfonso, who prized it as one of his greatest jewels. It eventually came to rest in the rich library of Don Diego de Mendoza <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish diplomat, book collector, and humanist</note>, and from there, King Philip II acquired it to enrich the library of the "eighth wonder of the world" <note>A traditional Spanish epithet for the Royal Site of San Lorenzo de El Escorial</note>.

It details the manuscript's provenance from the King's personal collection to the library of the Escorial.</summary>

See the general title: “Here begins the book of the forms and of the images that are in the heavens, and of the virtues and of the works that proceed from them into the bodies that are below the heaven of the moon <note>This refers to the "sublunary sphere," a concept in ancient cosmology where the Earth and its elements are influenced by the movements of the celestial bodies above</note>: which the very high and honored Lord ALFONSO, lover of sciences and of knowledge, by the grace of God KING of Castile, of Toledo, of León, of Galicia, of Seville, of Córdoba, of Murcia, of Jaén, and of the Algarve, and son of the very honored KING Lord FERNANDO, and of the QUEEN Lady BEATRIZ, ordered to be composed from the books of the ancient philosophers. And this book was begun in the 25th year of his reign. And in the Era of Caesar <note>The Spanish Era or Era of Caesar was a dating system used in the Iberian Peninsula that began in 38 BC; to find the Year of our Lord (AD), one subtracts 38 from the Era year</note>, in one thousand three hundred and fourteen years. And in that of our Lord Jesus Christ, in one thousand two hundred and seventy-six years. And it was finished in the 27th year of his reign. And in the Era of Caesar, in one thousand three hundred and seventeen years. And in that of our Lord Jesus Christ, in one thousand two hundred and seventy-nine years.”

The first part “is by Abolays <note>Likely a reference to a legendary or semi-historical Arabic source, possibly related to the scholar Aly Aben Ragel</note>, which speaks of the images and of their works that are made in stones through the degrees of the twelve signs; and it contains three hundred and sixty chapters.” This is the portion kept in the Escorial Library and which now enters the public domain. The others were by Tintim, Pythagoras, Xluz, Belyeno, Pliny Utarit, Ragiel, Yacoth, and Aly: all refer to the virtues and use of stones, to their relationship with the signs of heaven, and to their influence on the birth and fate of men.

This does not seem the occasion to judge, either literarily or scientifically, the first part which *speaks of three hundred and sixty stones, noble and base, precious and common*, and of their virtues, properties, and characters. It is supposed to have been written originally in Chaldean <note>A term often used historically to refer to Aramaic or ancient Babylonian languages</note>, translated into Arabic by the wise rabbi Abolays, lost afterwards for a long time, and finally found and possessed by the immortal author of *Las Partidas* <term>Las Siete Partidas: A foundational legal code of Castile compiled during the reign of Alfonso X</term>, who commissioned the cleric Garci-Perez to produce the Castilian version, so that men might better understand the book and know how to take advantage of it.

Now made accessible to the public by the marvelous auxiliary arts of the printing press, men of science will investigate what Mineralogy and Chemistry, Physics and Medicine might owe to it today; philologists will compare the language of the *Lapidary* with that of the *Books of Astronomical Knowledge*, and with that of the legal works and treatises, arriving at a precise understanding of the general state of the Castilian tongue in the second half of the 13th century, and whether it obeyed a uniform system, or varied, or was made unique according to the genius, taste, education, and science of each writer, among the many who assisted the...

Wise King <note>A title for Alfonso X of Castile, known for his vast intellectual contributions</note> in his colossal scientific and literary undertakings. Only then will
well-founded criticism be able to determine if the King himself provided unity and harmonious
connection to such diverse works, making them his own in a certain way, or if
on the contrary he left them with the lack of coordination in plan, method, and style, which
we see diminish much of what is written today in collaboration.

With what has been said thus far, the importance and significance of the
very interesting publication undertaken by Messrs. Fernandez Montaña, Selfa,
and Rodrigañez is clearly justified. The philologist <term>philologist: a scholar of language and historical texts</term>, the naturalist, the stu-
dent—in a word—must be extremely grateful that what until now had to be
considered an unknown and sterile bibliographic curiosity has become
public domain.

But the artist, the poet, and the historian shall be no less grateful for the
most faithful reproduction of the codex <term>codex: an ancient manuscript in book form</term>. This consists of 119 leaves, or 238 pa-
ges in folio; 226 with two vignettes and two capital letters, richly and beautifully
adorned. The book is divided by the twelve signs of the Zodiac; and at the beginning
of each one of them, the corresponding sign occupies the entire page,
surrounded by the respective constellations, and embraced all around by the empyrean
heaven with the angelic choirs. The influence that the ancients supposed the
stars to exert over each and every earthly being is well known.
The sign of the Zodiac is depicted according to what has been attributed to it since antiquity; and to
it, the objects that are the subject of each particular chapter bear a greater or
lesser resemblance, giving occasion to a beautiful variety within unity itself,
a variety so much to the taste of ingenious artists in the Middle Ages.

The two vignettes of the other pages allude to the principal matter that
is elucidated there; just as the two capital letters take as their subject the place
where and how the corresponding stone of the 360 is found, and the miner,
the fisherman, or the lucky inventor who presents it to the philosopher. The latter appears
almost always immersed in study. From here comes the vivid artistic, his-
torical, and poetic interest of the publication, where minutely and with their own
colors are portrayed cities, castles and temples, furniture, costumes of Moors
and Christians, weapons, vessels, tools and instruments of farming and
mining, the attack and defense of very high towers, anatomical dissections <note>original: "autopsias cadavéricas"</note>;
in short, everything that was a reflection of material life in that century.

The great Latin master of rules <note>This refers to the Roman poet Horace</note> already said that the ears are more sluggish in
seizing upon things than the eyes, for a perceptive gaze understands
and makes its own at a single stroke that which through the ear requires a long and sometimes

...intricate explanation, which is naturally tiresome. Here, then, the historian, the artist, and the poet find an arsenal of priceless data, which they will grasp and make use of on the fly simply by having the book on their table.

This is enough reason for the Royal Academy of History to recommend, with the greatest interest and effectiveness, this work for official protection <note>This likely refers to state sponsorship or institutional funding to ensure the project's completion and distribution</note>, as it provides such powerful aid both to our historical institute and to many other most important branches of human knowledge. All sciences and all speculations of the mind are linked, intertwined, and help one another, to the point that it is impossible for one to live entirely divorced from the others.

The character of the publication we are examining is such that any of the Royal Academies could speak of the whole work without risk of error. The editors limit themselves to doing what a mirror does physically: reproducing with total accuracy and identity the object placed before it. Just as a mirror reduces size due to distance, the editors reduce the writing of a page that measures 31 centimeters in the original to 22; but even so, it still appears exactly as it is in itself. They have acted wisely, then, in adopting a proportionate and convenient size for this publication.

Neither the skilled artisan Don Antonio Selfa, nor our learned Corresponding Member Don José Fernandez Montaña, wished to give a merely picturesque or easy reproduction of the codex—representing the pitiful state it shows in many parts due to having been soaked and ruined during the horrific fire of the previous century <note>A reference to the 1772 fire at the Royal Library of the Monastery of El Escorial, which destroyed or damaged thousands of precious manuscripts</note>—instead, they both restored it with a master's hand. Pages 1, 28, 29, and from 41 to 46 are those that suffered most, with the text being almost erased in many places. The modern artist and the learned <term>paleographer: a scholar who specializes in deciphering, reading, and dating historical handwriting</term> pursued the traces of every word by sheer force of sight, with such success that not even once have they misread or guessed incorrectly, as has been minutely verified by one of the undersigned academics themselves. From this come the well-deserved praises from foreigners who visit that Library and take pleasure in examining this excellent reproduction. If <term>chromolithography: a 19th-century chemical process for printing multi-color images using a different stone for each ink color</term>, by using various stones for the printing, incurs small and insignificant misalignments—since an adjustment so perfect that the reproduction rivals the colors of a <term>camera obscura: an optical device that led to the invention of photography, used here to describe a perfectly projected image</term> is quite impossible—one would need the eyes of a lynx to notice them in a most scrupulous comparison of the original and the copy.

<meta>This page concludes the report by the Royal Academy of History regarding the facsimile edition of Alfonso X’s Lapidary. Following the discussion of the reproduction's scale and accuracy, the authors now highlight a significant discovery regarding the manuscript's missing opening pages and the rare portrait of the King they contain.</meta>

One more highlight of great value is present in this publication, which has not been fully appreciated until now. The book does not begin where it seems; it lacks the first pages or vellums <term>vitelas: high-quality calfskin parchment used for important manuscripts</term> which contain the heading and the index. Fortunately, these exist, as has been said, though they are bound separately as a distinct codex. The editors have correctly placed them at the start of the publication; for the vignette <note>a small illustration or portrait found at the beginning of a section</note> provides us with something worthy of great consideration: the portrait of King Alfonso X "the Wise." Here, he is shown not in the bloom and vigor of youth, but in the final years of his life, old and gray-haired. It could not be otherwise, for in 1276 and 1279, when the copy was begun and finished, the King was 53 and 56 years old respectively. He died in 1284.

Taking into account, then, the utility and importance of the publication, the sacrifices and expenses it entails, and that this is not one of those works where the public rewards the author or editor as amply and deservedly as they should, it falls to the Government to grant it decisive protection <note>This refers to state financial support or sponsorship to ensure the work reaches public institutions</note>. *The Lapidary of the Wise King Alfonso X*, photolithographed <term>photolithography: a 19th-century process used to create exact replicas of manuscripts by transferring images onto stone plates</term> and rivaling the original itself, must not and cannot be absent from public libraries, for the general instruction and benefit of scholars and the informed.

The Academy, however, shall resolve as it sees fit.

->AURELIANO FERNÁNDEZ-GUERRA. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; PEDRO DE MADRAZO.<-

# OF THE SIGN OF ARIES

<note>Aries is the first sign of the zodiac, representing the ram. In medieval science, the study of stones was deeply linked to the position of the stars.</note>

Aristotle, who was the most accomplished of all the philosophers and the one who most naturally demonstrated all things through true reason—and made them to be fully understood as they truly are—said that all things that exist under the heavens move and are directed by the movement of the celestial bodies through the **virtue** <term>virtue: in this context, it refers to a natural or occult power or property inherent in an object, influenced by the stars.</term> they receive from them, as ordained by God, who is the First Truth, and upon whom all other truths depend. And he showed that all things in the world are, as it were, linked together, receiving power from one another: the most lowly from the most noble.

And this power appears more manifest in some things, such as in animals and in plants, and more hidden in others, such as in stones and in metals. Concerning these things, the sages wrote books in which they spoke of the celestial bodies—which are not composed of the four elements <note>The four elements are earth, water, air, and fire. Medieval science taught that heavenly bodies were made of a "fifth element" or quintessence.</note>—and likewise of the other things composed of them, such as animals, which are all living things that have a soul capable of feeling and moving. And likewise of the plants that come from the fruits born of the earth, such as trees and herbs. And they spoke also of the harder things that are made of the earth, such as stones and metals.

And they made books about each of these. But those who spoke of stones, such as Aristotle—who wrote a book in which he named seven hundred of them—described the color of each one, its size, the virtue it possessed, and the place where it could be found. And many other sages who touched upon these matters did the same. However, among those, there were some who delved deeper into the study of them, holding that it was not

<column-break/>

enough simply to know their color, size, or virtue, unless they also knew which celestial bodies they were connected to and from which they received the virtue that directed them to perform their works, according to the alignment of the states of the bodies above, in every manner of good or evil.

Among the sages who worked most on this was one named **Abolays**. <note>original: "Abolays". This is likely a Castilian transcription of an Arabic name, possibly Abu al-Ays, a scholar of whom little is known outside this text.</note> And although he held the law of the Moors <note>The "law of the Moors" refers to Islam.</note>, he was a man who greatly loved the Gentiles <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers to the ancient pre-Islamic civilizations, specifically the pagans of antiquity.</note>, and especially those of the land of **Chaldea** <term>Chaldea: an ancient region in Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) famous in the Middle Ages for its advanced knowledge of astronomy and magic.</term>, for his ancestors were from there. And because he knew how to speak that language and read their script, he took great pains to seek out their books and study them, for he had heard it said that in that land were the greatest sages in all the world. But because of the great wars and the many other misfortunes that occurred there, the people’s knowledge was largely lost, so that very little of it could be found.

And this Abolays had a friend who helped him with these books and obtained them for him. And among those he sought out, he found this book of three hundred and sixty stones, according to the degrees of the signs that are in the **eighth heaven**. <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the "eighth heaven" or eighth sphere is the firmament containing the fixed stars, located beyond the spheres of the seven planets.</note> And it told of the color, name, and virtue of each one, and in what place the star of the constellation was found—the one located in the degree of that sign from which the stone receives its strength and virtue.

And this is according to how the sun runs throughout the year through the degrees of the figures of the twelve signs, which total three hundred and sixty; these are all represented by small stars and many other figures that are in the eighth heaven. These are also shaped by stars: some toward the north, which is by the star they call the **Trasmontana** <note>The North Star or Polaris.</note>, and others toward the south, some within the signs and others outside of them, so that including the signs, they total forty-eight constellations. Therefore, when Abolays found this book, he was very joyful, for in it he found everything he had desired to find regarding this knowledge of stones. And after he had read it much and understood what was in it, he **translated it from the Chaldean language into Arabic**. And during his life, he strove to test those things contained within it and found them certain and true, for he was a master of the art of astronomy and of the nature of knowing stones. And after he died, this book remained as if lost for a very long time, so that those who possessed it...

And he found it in Segovia, as a Prince during the life of his father, in the year that he won the Kingdom of Murcia, which was in the Era of <note>The "Spanish Era" was a dating system used in the Iberian Peninsula; the text leaves the specific year blank here, though historical records suggest 1243–1250 AD.</note>

He held it in Toledo, having obtained it from a Jew who kept it hidden, not wishing to make use of it himself nor wanting it to be of benefit to any other. And once he had this book in his power, he had it read by another of his Jews, who was his physician and was called **Yehuda Mosca the Younger**, who was very learned in the art of astronomy and knew and understood both Arabic and Latin well. And once he had understood, through this Jew his physician, the good and the great benefit that lay within it, he ordered it to be translated from Arabic into the Castilian language so that men might understand it better and know how to take greater advantage of it. And in this translation, he was assisted by **Garci Pérez**, one of his clerics, who was likewise very learned in this knowledge of astronomy. And the translation was finished in the second year after the noble King Ferdinand, his father, won the city of Seville <note>Seville was conquered in 1248; the translation was thus completed around 1250.</note>.

And this book is very noble and very precious; and whoever wishes to make use of it must keep three things in mind. **The first** is that they be knowledgeable in astronomy, so that they may know how to recognize the stars, what state they are in, and at what season the greatest **virtue** <term>virtue: the inherent natural power or "astrological charge" of an object</term> comes to the stones from them—second only to the virtue they receive from God. **The second thing** is that they know how to recognize the stones, their colors, and their features, and likewise that they know certainly the designated places where they are formed and where they are found, and how to distinguish the counterfeit from the natural. They must also refine those which naturally resemble one another in appearance, distinguishing them by weight, hardness, and the other signs by which they can be known to a man who is learned in this knowledge. **The third thing** is that they be knowledgeable in the art of **physics** <term>physics: here meaning natural science and medicine</term>, for much of the power lies in the virtue of the stones as shown in this book; let them know how to work with them, just as in the <unclear>mantar</unclear>, having the sound judgment to know how to help themselves with things that bring benefit and guard against those that bring harm. And working in this manner, one will reach what they desire

This is the lodestone or magnet.</note>

This stone has a natural virtue in itself to pull iron with very great force. sea to the ships that pass near it, it pulls all their nails from them by force from the direction where the rock <note>Original: "pienna," meaning a rocky crag or cliff.</note> is, in such a way that it makes the nails fly like arrows. And if they are so well-riveted that the stone cannot stretch or pull them out, it makes the ships move against the rock so fiercely that they break upon the stones and perish. And it is a great marvel that iron, which conquers all other metals by the strength it possesses, is conquered by this stone through its natural property <note>Original: "ppiedat," here referring to the innate "pity" or "attraction" of the stone's nature.</note>, making the iron come to it obediently. And by this, it is shown that this attraction is more by the force of opposition than by likeness. So great is the virtue <term>virtue: in medieval science, this refers to an inherent power or medicinal property</term> that the iron receives from this stone—if the stone is of fine quality—that the iron itself pulls other smaller pieces of iron to it, so that they cling to it just as they do to the stone. In this way, it can pull many pieces of iron, clinging one to another in as great a quantity as the first can support. This virtue is so proven and so manifest that, beyond what a man sees with his eyes, by holding the stone in one hand and the iron in the other, he feels how the iron seeks to join with the stone, and one iron with another. And if a man wishes for this stone to lose its virtue, let him put it in the juice of garlic or onions so that it is entirely covered for three days and three nights, and it will lose it. And if he wishes for it to recover its power, let him put it for another three days and three nights in the blood of a he-goat <note>Goat's blood was often cited in medieval lapidaries as a substance capable of softening diamonds or recharging magnets.</note> that is likewise kept open, and it will recover it, provided the blood is changed every day. And in this stone there is also another great marvel: if it is placed in a clay pot in a furnace of strong fire, and this is done four times, changing the pot for a new one each time, once it is burnt and taken from the furnace, and a little sulfur is placed beside it and the stone is sprinkled with water, a fire so strong will come out of it that it will burn from a great distance anything it reaches that is flammable. This happens because the stone is hot and dry; and when they burn it, the virtue of fire is ignited within it and hidden. Therefore, it flees from water, which is its opposite (being cold and wet), and joins with the sulfur, which is its likeness (being hot and dry). In this way, it is repelled very fiercely by its contrary, which is stronger than itself, and joining with great force to its like, it burns very intensely as was said above. And if a man wishes for it to lose this burning quality, let him pour any kind of oil over it, and it will lose it. And

<column-break/>

this stone has a virtue in itself: that he who carries it with him, if he be a man faint of heart, it will give him courage; and if he is already brave, it will strengthen him more. And in the art of medicine <note>Original: "fisica," referring to the work of a physician or natural philosopher.</note> it is very profitable: for if any man is given iron filings to drink, or any other kind of poison in which iron is mixed, or if he is wounded by a poisoned iron weapon, by grinding this stone into powder and mixing it with whatever oil one wishes and giving it to drink to the one who is poisoned, it will draw the poison out from below <note>A euphemism for purging the bowels.</note> and he will be healed immediately. It will do the same if the ground stone is placed upon the wound of one who has been poisoned. And he who wishes to know with which stars this stone has its connection, and from which it receives its strength and virtue: let him know that they are those three stars that are in the face <note>The "face" refers to a specific decan or subdivision of a zodiac sign.</note> and follow the knot of the cord of the figure of Pisces <note>In the constellation of Pisces, the two fish are traditionally depicted as being tied together by a cord or ribbon.</note>; and one of them is at the end of the tail of one fish. And the proof that these stars have the power to pull iron is the virtue the stone receives from them. And when the middle star of these three rises on the eastern horizon, the stone will have greater force and more virtue in all those works we have mentioned.

**T**he fourth degree of the sign of Aries: is the stone they call **miliziz** <note>original: "miliziz"</note>. Which means as much in Chaldean <note>The language of ancient Babylonia</note> as: "ripener of abscesses." This stone is found in the mountain that is near the House of the Temple <note>Refers to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem</note> in certain places that resemble caves; whoever enters inside, their body feels the heat of a bath and a smell like smoke. And there are of these stones both large and small: and those that have white mixed with the purple are the best. And when they polish this stone, it becomes as smooth as other stones. And it has such virtue <term>virtue: an inherent natural power or medicinal property</term> that it draws the impurities from the water <note>original: "suzies dela aguia," possibly referring to sediment or specific fluids</note>: just as the lodestone <term>lodestone: a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</term> draws iron. And in the matter of medicine <note>original: "fisica"</note> it works great benefit: for he who grinds it and kneads it with some liquid and places it over an abscess <term>abscess: a swollen, inflamed area of body tissue, often called a 'postema' in the original text</term>: it makes it ripen immediately; and if he hangs it over it, it does the same. And whoever wishes to do evil with it and gives it to someone to drink in the weight of six drachmas <term>drachma: an ancient unit of weight, roughly 3.4 grams</term>: they will die from a potent poison <note>original: "venino del rre diurso," likely implying a complex or diverse-acting toxin</note>. But if they take less of it, the size of a caper <note>original: "capiri"</note>: it will be understood that he who gave it to drink did no harm; rather, it will do much good. This stone is by its nature hot and dry. And it receives its power from the strength of the southern star of the three that are upon the loin of the **Chained Woman** <note>The constellation Andromeda</note> who never knew a husband. **Of the stone they call monetoz: .vi.**

The sixth degree of the sign of Aries is the stone that is called **monetoz** <note>original: "monetoz"</note>. It has this name because when they pound it and take what comes out of it and give it to a pregnant woman to hold, the child dies immediately: and it makes it [the child] come out dead or alive <note>original: "faze la a t'ra muerta o vina," meaning the stone induces labor or expulsion</note>, in whatever state it might be. And it does this same thing if she carries it hung upon her. And from such a reputation, they take animals that come from her <note>referring to the offspring of livestock</note> or hang it above them. This virtue <term>virtue: an inherent natural power or medicinal property</term> is bad for women who have living children in their wombs and do not wish to lose them; and good for those who have dead children and cannot cast them out, or are so weak that they cannot give birth. And the color of this stone is a mixture of green with red. But its greenness is so weak that it tends toward yellow, and likewise the redness is so little that it resembles the water of meat when it is placed in salt <note>likely referring to a pale, pinkish-red brine</note>. And its mine is in the reefs <note>original: "rreznas"</note> of the islands of the sea that are in the land they call Çin <note>China</note>. And by its nature it is hot and dry. And the star that follows the one in the turn of the River <note>referring to the constellation Eridanus, the River</note> has power over this stone, and from it its strength and virtue are born. And when it is in the ascendant <term>ascendant: the zodiac sign or star rising on the eastern horizon</term>, this stone shows its works more clearly.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Within the large decorative letter D at the top right, a miniature shows two men; one is seated in a blue robe gesturing toward a standing man in a brown tunic. Below the text column, a large square miniature depicts the zodiac sign Aries as a ram with a dappled coat, surrounded by blue circles containing red dots representing stars.</image-desc>

**Of the stone they call gotitiz: .vii.**

The seventh degree of the sign of Aries: is the stone they call **gotitiz** <note>original: "gotitiz"</note>. And it has this name from a river that is so called where they find it on the shores of the Indian Sea. And because it is not found in any other place but there, for that reason it has no other name except after the river. Of nature it is hot and dry. And its color is green mixed with yellow, but the yellow is more than the green. And the proof of it is that if they take a weight of ten drachms <term>drachm: an ancient unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</term> [of this stone] and place it near copper or brass <note>original: "cobre o arambre"</note> weighing half a drachm, just as the lodestone <term>lodestone: a naturally magnetic piece of the mineral magnetite</term> draws iron according to its quantity, it draws more or less. And it has yet another virtue: that if they take a weight of half a drachm and throw it over ten [drachms] of molten silver, it will turn it a yellow color; and if they do this three or four times, it turns into the color of pure gold and will withstand the melting of fire forevermore; but it is not natural gold. And it does this because there is in it the nature of red sulfur <note>original: "sufre uermeio"</note>. And in the art of medicine <note>original: "fisica"</note> it has this virtue: that if one takes the weight of two grains of achor <note>original: "achor," likely a specific seed or small measure of weight</note>, grinds them, and mixes them with fresh water, and puts it in the nostrils of one who is born with the illness they call tremorio <note>tremors or shaking fits</note>, they will heal at the first time, or at the latest, the second. And the leading star of the three that are in the Horn of the sign of Aries, and the other which is in the neck of this figure, have power over this stone, and from them it receives its virtue. And when these stars are in the ascendant, this stone shows its works more clearly.

### Of the stone they call letimmuz . . . .

<image-desc>A rectangular miniature with a decorative border. Inside, two figures are depicted against an orange background. Of the eighth degree of the sign of Aries: it is the stone they call **letimmuz** <note>original: "letimmuz"</note>. This stone is by its nature hot and dry: and its dryness is in the fourth degree <note>this refers to the medieval medical system of "degrees," where the fourth degree was the highest level of intensity for a quality</note>. It is black in color: and there appears in it a bit of redness: so that it resembles peppercorns. It is strong and very hard, so that it cannot be broken with anything except yellow brass that is dyed with the **tutty of Alexandria** <term>tutty: a crude zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces, used in medieval alchemy and medicine</term>: and this breaks it in such a way that as soon as the brass touches the stone, it breaks immediately. This is found in the land of the blacks on the bank of a river that passes through those places where these stones are: and they find them there of various colors and shapes. But they find it always in a round form: and flat, shaped like a shell <note>original: "coxuella"</note>: and some of them are large and some small. And its virtue <term>virtue: an inherent natural power or medicinal property</term> is very useful in the art of medicine <note>original: "fisica," referring to the natural sciences and healing</note>. For if they place it upon a wound or a sore, it heals very quickly without forming poison <note>referring to infection or pus</note> or an abscess. And if they hang it over [the wound], it does this same thing. And the star that is upon the head of the figure of the woman who is seated in the chair <note>referring to the constellation Cassiopeia</note>: and the other that is in the fold <note>original: "recobrado"</note> of that same figure, which they call the **dyed palm** <note>original: "la palma tinta," a translation of the Arabic name for the star Caph, meaning the "stained hand" of the constellation</note>, have power over this stone, and from them it receives its force and virtue. And when both are in the **ascendant** <term>ascendant: the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term>: this stone shows its works more clearly: . . . . . . . . .

### Of the stone they call anititiaz . . . .

Of the ninth degree of the sign of Aries: it is the stone they call **anititiaz** <note>original: "anititiaz"</note>. This is by its nature hot and dry. And they find it in the islands of a land named Can: in a place near where they say the **River of Honey** <note>original: "ryo dela miel"</note> flows. This stone is light in weight and very porous: and they never find it except in a square shape. It is red in color but not much, for a large part of it tends toward a yellow color: and there are those who find them entirely yellow. And its property is such that if they polish it with something, a flavor as sweet as honey comes from it. And in the art of medicine it is of great benefit. For if they give it to drink to a man who has a cough or another ailment of the chest: it is of very great benefit and he heals immediately. And if they hang it over that place where the ailment is: it does the same, but not so quickly. And the leading star of the three following ones that are in the figure of the **River** <note>referring to the constellation Eridanus</note> has power over this stone: and from it, it receives its force and virtue. ### Of the stone that flees from milk: . . . . .

<image-desc>A circular miniature set within a decorative gold-bordered square. Inside, a man in a red tunic and a man in a yellow robe are depicted in an interior setting. One man gestures toward a table holding several small dark objects, likely the stones described in the text.</image-desc>

**O**f the thirteenth degree of the sign of Aries: it is the stone that flees from the milk. This stone is hot and dry by its nature. It is black in color: and so porous that it floats <note>original: "naue," literally "ships" or "navigates," meaning it is buoyant enough to float</note> for that reason. It is rough to the touch and easy to break. It is found on the bank of a river named Durla <note>possibly a localized name for a branch of the Nile</note> which is in the land of Egypt. And its property is such that if it is placed near the milk of any animal, the stone jumps and flees far from it, so that in no way does it wish to be joined with it. And all this is because of the enmity it has with milk according to its nature. This stone is very good in the art of medicine <term>physics: the medieval term for medicine and the study of natural properties</term>, for if it is ground and mixed with vinegar and used to anoint the bite of any white or black viper <note>original: "morsegas de alua o negra," referring to the bites of specific venomous serpents</note>, it heals it immediately. And the star that is in the right knee of the **Chained Woman** <note>the constellation Andromeda</note> has power and lordship over this stone, and from it, the stone receives its strength and virtue. And when that star is in the ascendant, this stone will manifest its works most clearly.
